props.title: Cat People
props.initialSlug: A woman fears her passion will turn her into a killer cat

sections.content: Cat People (1942) revolutionized psychological horror through suggestion rather than spectacle. Producer Val Lewton and director Jacques Tourneur crafted a masterclass in shadows and sound, proving that imagination trumps explicit scares. The film's legendary pool scene and bus scare ("Lewton bus") created templates for jump scares still used today. This influenced later psychological thrillers like Rosemary's Baby (1968) and The Innocents (1961), showing how supernatural terror could emerge from everyday urban settings.

sections.content: The film's exploration of female sexuality and repression was groundbreaking for 1942. Simone Simon's Irena embodies cultural fears about feminine power and "otherness" that would later influence films like The Black Cat (1934) and The Seventh Victim (1943). Tourneur's technique of keeping the supernatural elements ambiguous created a template for psychological horror that echoes through Don't Look Now (1973) and The Devil's Backbone (2001).

Lewton's production unit at RKO created a string of sophisticated B-movies that elevated horror beyond monster movies. Their approach influenced directors like Mario Bava (Black Sunday, 1960) and Jacques Tourneur's own later work like Night of the Demon (1957). The emphasis on psychological dread over physical horror created a new language for expressing fear on screen. SUBHEAD: The Lewton Legacy

The film's technical innovations in sound design and shadow play directly influenced film noir and modern horror. The famous swimming pool scene, with its creative use of shadows and sound effects, established techniques still studied in film schools. Later directors like Roman Polanski (Repulsion, 1965) and Guillermo del Toro (The Shape of Water, 2017) have acknowledged their debt to Lewton's sophisticated approach to supernatural themes.
